lead: This unit explains how a CMOS inverter behaves at DC and in time, and how that behaviour decides the speed, power and logic style of a digital chip. After it you can read a voltage transfer curve, estimate delay and power, size transistors, and compare static, ratioed, pass-transistor and dynamic logic.
about: Chapters 3.1 and 3.2 start with the CMOS inverter and the older NMOS loads, using the voltage transfer curve to define switching threshold and noise margins. Chapter 3.3 turns to switching: capacitances, rise and fall times, and propagation delay. Chapter 3.4 puts numbers on delay with logical effort and transistor sizing. Chapters 3.5 and 3.6 cover where power goes and how to cut it. The last three chapters compare circuit styles: static CMOS and ratioed logic in 3.7, pass-transistor logic and transmission gates in 3.8, and dynamic, domino and cascode voltage switch logic in 3.9. Each style is judged by the same measures: swing, delay, power and area.

chapters.idea: The CMOS inverter's voltage transfer curve gives the switching threshold, the logic levels and the noise margins.
chapters.depth: Derive the VTC from nMOS and pMOS drain currents in the five regions. Define V<sub>OH</sub>, V<sub>OL</sub>, V<sub>IL</sub>, V<sub>IH</sub>, V<sub>M</sub>, NM<sub>H</sub> and NM<sub>L</sub>. Show the matched-inverter case and the effect of β<sub>n</sub>/β<sub>p</sub>. Some syllabi call the curve the DC transfer characteristic or the butterfly curve when drawn for both directions.

figure.aria: A voltage transfer curve that stays high, falls steeply through the middle, and stays low.

chapters.example: A matched CMOS inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 3.3 V, V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.6 V, |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.6 V and equal β. Find V<sub>M</sub> and the state of both transistors at V<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>M</sub>. At V<sub>M</sub> both devices are in saturation, so V<sub>M</sub> = (V<sub>DD</sub> + V<sub>tn</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|)/2 = 1.65 V.
chapters.trap: Assuming V<sub>M</sub> is always V<sub>DD</sub>/2: a larger β<sub>n</sub> pulls V<sub>M</sub> down, and the pMOS overdrive is V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>in</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|, not V<sub>in</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for MOS regions and drain-current equations; Unit 2 for the CMOS cross-section.
chapters.leave: Detailed fabrication, layout and transistor I-V derivation go to Units 1 and 2.

chapters.idea: An NMOS inverter needs a load; the four common loads trade output low voltage, static current and speed.
chapters.depth: Cover resistive, enhancement NMOS, depletion NMOS and pseudo-nMOS loads. For each, draw the load line, find V<sub>OL</sub> and V<sub>OH</sub>, and note whether the load is always on. Some syllabi call pseudo-nMOS a ratioed inverter or an always-on pMOS load. Keep the treatment at the DC level; delay comes in 3.3.

figure.aria: A tree grouping the four NMOS inverter loads under one root.

chapters.example: A resistive-load NMOS inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V, R<sub>L</sub> = 100 kΩ, k<sub>n</sub> = 20 µA/V² and V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.8 V. The input is at 5 V. Find V<sub>OL</sub>. The driver is in linear region: (5 − V<sub>OL</sub>)/100 kΩ = 20 µA/V²[(5 − 0.8)V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2]; solving gives V<sub>OL</sub> ≈ 0.57 V.
chapters.trap: Using the saturation equation for the driver when V<sub>OL</sub> is small; the driver is in linear region. Also forgetting that depletion and pseudo-nMOS loads conduct with zero input.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for the CMOS VTC; Unit 1 for nMOS regions.
chapters.leave: CMOS inverter noise margins are in 3.1; dynamic switching is in 3.3.

chapters.idea: Switching delay comes from charging and discharging the load capacitance through the finite drive current of the transistors.
chapters.depth: Define t<sub>PHL</sub>, t<sub>PLH</sub>, t<sub>p</sub>, rise time and fall time. Use the average-current method and the RC approximation. Explain input capacitance, output capacitance and Miller effect briefly. Some syllabi call this transient response or AC characteristics.

figure.aria: Timing diagram: the output falls 0.5 ns after the input rises.

chapters.example: A CMOS inverter drives C<sub>L</sub> = 50 fF. k<sub>n</sub> = 200 µA/V², V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V and V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.5 V. Estimate t<sub>PHL</sub> using half the saturation current as the average current. I<sub>Dsat</sub> = (k<sub>n</sub>/2)(V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>)² = 169 µA; t<sub>PHL</sub> ≈ C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>/(2I<sub>Dsat</sub>) = 0.27 ns.
chapters.trap: Swapping t<sub>PHL</sub> and t<sub>PLH</sub>; t<sub>PHL</sub> is output high-to-low, driven by the nMOS. Also using the full saturation current instead of an average current.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for the inverter; Unit 1 for capacitances.
chapters.leave: Logical effort and path delay are in 3.4; power is in 3.5.

chapters.idea: Logical effort turns a gate-level path into a delay estimate and tells you how to size each stage.
chapters.depth: Define logical effort g, parasitic delay p, electrical effort f, path effort F, branch effort b and stage effort. Give g and p for inverter, NAND2, NOR2. Size a path for equal stage effort. Some syllabi call this the method of logical effort or path delay optimisation.

figure.aria: Two straight lines: NAND2 has a higher intercept and a steeper slope than an inverter.

chapters.example: A path is inverter → 2-input NAND → inverter, driving a load of 64 input capacitances. G = 1 × (4/3) × 1 = 4/3, H = 64, so F = G H = 85.33. Stage effort f = F<sup>1/3</sup> = 4.4. P = 1 + 2 + 1 = 4, so D = 3 × 4.4 + 4 = 17.2 τ.
chapters.trap: Forgetting branch effort when a node drives two paths; or adding parasitic delay after multiplication instead of inside the path sum.
chapters.leave: Transistor-level SPICE delay and interconnect delay are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: CMOS power has a dynamic part from switching and short-circuit current, and a static part from leakage.
chapters.depth: Derive P<sub>dyn</sub> = α C V<sub>DD</sub>² f and P<sub>sc</sub>. List subthreshold, gate-oxide and junction leakage. Define activity factor. Some syllabi call static power standby power or leakage power.

figure.aria: A tree splitting power into dynamic and static parts, with switching, short-circuit and three leakage paths.

chapters.example: A CMOS chip has V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V, C = 50 pF, f = 100 MHz and activity α = 0.1. P<sub>dyn</sub> = α C V<sub>DD</sub>² f = 0.1 × 50 pF × 3.24 V² × 100 MHz = 1.62 mW. Leakage is 10 µA, so P<sub>leak</sub> = 18 µW and total power is 1.638 mW.
chapters.trap: Using C V<sub>DD</sub>² f without the activity factor, or treating leakage as zero at low frequency.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.3 for capacitance; Unit 1 for leakage.
chapters.leave: Low-power techniques are in 3.6; power-grid design is outside the unit.

chapters.idea: Low-power design cuts dynamic energy by lowering activity, capacitance or voltage, and cuts leakage by switching blocks off or using high-V<sub>t</sub> devices.
chapters.depth: Cover clock gating, power gating, DVFS, multi-V<sub>t</sub> cells and sleep modes. Explain the cost: wake-up latency and area. Some syllabi call this power management or low-power VLSI.

figure.aria: A control chain from workload to power manager to techniques to functional blocks.

chapters.example: DVFS changes V<sub>DD</sub> from 1.2 V to 1.0 V and frequency from 1 GHz to 0.8 GHz. Dynamic power scales as C V<sub>DD</sub>² f, so the ratio is (1.0/1.2)² × (0.8/1.0) = 0.556. The saving is 44.4%.
chapters.trap: Thinking power gating saves dynamic power during normal operation; it mainly cuts leakage while a block is off.
chapters.leave: Circuit-level power-grid and clock-tree design are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Static CMOS uses complementary networks so every output is driven to a rail; ratioed logic uses an always-on load and saves transistors at the cost of static current.
chapters.depth: Draw the complementary pull-up and pull-down networks. Define ratioed logic and explain V<sub>OL</sub> > 0. Compare transistor count, swing, static power and noise margin. Some syllabi call static CMOS complementary CMOS, and group tristate and clocked CMOS here as short variants.

figure.aria: A tree comparing complementary static CMOS with two ratioed loads.

chapters.example: A pseudo-nMOS inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 2.5 V, k<sub>n</sub> = 100 µA/V², V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.5 V, k<sub>p</sub> = 20 µA/V² and |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.5 V. The pMOS gate is at 0 V. Find V<sub>OL</sub> and the static current. The load is in saturation: I<sub>load</sub> = (20 µA/V²/2)(2.5 − 0.5)² = 40 µA. The driver is in linear region: 40 µA = 100 µA/V²[(2.5 − 0.5)V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2], giving V<sub>OL</sub> ≈ 0.21 V.
chapters.trap: Assuming a ratioed gate has zero static power; the load conducts whenever the output is low. Also using the driver's saturation equation when V<sub>OL</sub> is small.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for the inverter; Chapter 3.2 for pseudo-nMOS.
chapters.leave: Pass-transistor and dynamic styles are in 3.8 and 3.9.

chapters.idea: A pass transistor switches a signal by connecting it to the output, but an nMOS alone loses a threshold voltage; a transmission gate adds a pMOS to pass the full rail.
chapters.depth: Explain nMOS and pMOS pass transistors, threshold drop, body effect, and the parallel nMOS-pMOS transmission gate. Give the TG symbol and truth table. Some syllabi call this PTL or complementary pass-transistor logic when several branches are used.

figure.aria: A data path through a transmission gate, with nMOS and pMOS control inputs.

chapters.example: An nMOS pass transistor has V<sub>in</sub> = 3.3 V, gate at 3.3 V and V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.6 V. The maximum output is V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub> = 2.7 V. A transmission gate adds a pMOS and passes the full 3.3 V.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the V<sub>tn</sub> drop on a high input; the drop also rises with body effect when the source is not at ground.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for threshold and body effect; Chapter 3.7 for static CMOS.
chapters.leave: Dynamic logic and domino are in 3.9; full adder design is in Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Dynamic logic uses a clocked precharge and evaluate cycle; domino adds an inverter to make cascades work, and CVSL uses a cross-coupled pMOS pair.
chapters.depth: Draw precharge and evaluate phases, charge sharing, keeper transistors, the domino non-inverting rule and CVSL. Compare with static CMOS. Some syllabi call domino logic clocked CMOS, and NORA or TSPC appear as clocked dynamic families; only a few universities teach NORA and TSPC in detail.

figure.aria: A clocked timeline: precharge while the clock is low, evaluate while it is high.

chapters.example: A dynamic node C<sub>dyn</sub> = 50 fF is precharged to 1.8 V. An internal node C<sub>int</sub> = 10 fF starts at 0 V and connects during evaluation. Find the final voltage with no keeper. Charge is conserved: V = (50 fF × 1.8 V)/(60 fF) = 1.5 V.
chapters.trap: Cascading dynamic gates without domino inverters; or ignoring charge sharing, which can flip the output even when the pull-down is off.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.3 for capacitance; Chapter 3.8 for pass transistors.
chapters.leave: Clocked storage elements and sequential logic are in Unit 4.
